pr.body: Adds member notification emails. The original PR says failed notifications should not undo the user action.
pr.title: Send Nika's email copy and add member notification emails

files.text:
# Notification emails are a courtesy: a failed send must not undo the action.
  def notify
    yield.deliver_now
  rescue StandardError => error
    Rails.logger.error("Notification delivery failed: #{error.class.name}")
  end

if @contact_request.save
      notify { MemberMailer.contacted(@contact_request) }
      notify { MemberMailer.request_received(@contact_request) }
      redirect_to profile_contact_thanks_path(@recipient.public_slug), status: :see_other
    else
      render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end

config.action_mailer.default_url_options = { host: ENV.fetch("APP_HOST", "commonbound.work"), protocol: "https" }
  config.action_mailer.delivery_method = :smtp
  config.action_mailer.raise_delivery_errors = true
  config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = {
    address: ENV.fetch("SMTP_ADDRESS", "localhost"),
    port: ENV.fetch("SMTP_PORT", "587").to_i,
    domain: ENV.fetch("SMTP_DOMAIN", "commonbound.org"),
    user_name: ENV["SMTP_USERNAME"], password: ENV["SMTP_PASSWORD"],
    authentication: :plain, enable_starttls: :always, openssl_verify_mode: "peer",
    open_timeout: 10, read_timeout: 10
  }

report.summary: Two curated conversations about separate latency and failure-handling trade-offs.

points.title: Decide how much waiting an email is worth
points.observation: After saving a contact request, the controller sends two emails before redirecting. Each notify call uses deliver_now, so this request waits for delivery to return or raise.
points.why: A slow SMTP response adds to the time this user waits. Rescuing a delivery error protects the saved action, but does not remove that wait.
points.question: How long should someone wait after sending a message, and how would we measure how much of that time is spent sending email?
points.principle: Decide from measured latency and product needs. Moving delivery to a queue can shorten the request, but adds retry behaviour and a worker to operate.
assumptions: No latency or traffic measurements were supplied. Inline delivery may be reasonable for the pilot.

evidence.quote:
def notify
    yield.deliver_now
  rescue StandardError => error
    Rails.logger.error("Notification delivery failed: #{error.class.name}")

points.title: Keep a saved action when a courtesy email fails
points.observation: The contact request is saved before notification begins. The shared notify helper catches StandardError from delivery, logs it and lets the action continue.
points.why: An email failure need not turn an already saved contact request into an error page. The same helper gives the controller actions a consistent way to handle these optional notifications.
points.question: Which parts of this action must succeed for the user, and which are optional? How would you test that a delivery exception still leaves the request saved and the response successful?
points.principle: Choose failure boundaries deliberately. Saving the core action and handling an optional side effect separately can preserve useful work when an external service fails.
assumptions: This praise applies to courtesy notifications. A login-code email has a different role and may need different failure handling.
